rules.requires: When all material failure in the run comes from one independent cause and the failed share is below the difficulty mode's loss, the score is 2 (Easy, FAIL, HOLD), even though the band table alone would give 3. A 3 needs a second independent miss or a failed share at or above the loss.

excerpts.text: - **Narrow-miss rule.** All material failure comes from one cause, and the failed share (about 5%) is below the Easy-mode loss (10%), so the narrow-miss rule sets the score to **2 (Easy, FAIL, HOLD)**.

Band table alone: F1 is one consequential misstatement that a bounded edit fixes, which could argue for 3. The narrow-miss rule decides it: one independent cause and a failed share of about 4%, below Easy's 10% loss, gives **2 (Easy)**. A 3 would need a second independent miss or a failed share at or above 10%.

**Difficulty mode:** medium, so the loss is 15% and the baseline limit is 85%. The central estimate is below the loss and there is only one cause, so the narrow-miss rule gives **2**, even though the band table alone would give 3.

rules.requires: /hardness reads the task's difficulty mode and applies a loss and a baseline limit for it: Easy has loss 10% and limit 90%, Medium has loss 15% and limit 85%. The failed share is compared with the loss. No stored report gives the Hard-mode figures.

rules.requires: The review estimates a failed share: the part of a weighted core answer that the run got wrong, stated as a percentage and usually with a range. One report gives the weights as 5 for traps and key reply numbers, 3 for standard decisions and deliverables and 1 for incidental ones.

rules.requires: Each report counts the independent causes of material failure. Causes are independent when they rest on different deciding records, in different services or places and about different items, and a run could make either miss without the other. The count is one of the two inputs to the narrow-miss rule.

excerpts.text: - **Independent causes: 2.** They rest on different deciding records (a Slack reply vs an Apple email), different items (a new cost line vs an existing issue) and different services. A run could make either one without the other.

**Independent causes of material failure: 3** (F1 Brian DM, F2 Gmail vendor notes, F3 ZOM-293 comment). Each rests on a different record in a different service or place, and the run could have made any one without the others.

**Independent causes: 2.** They rest on different deciding records in different services (a Gmail message vs a Slack DM with another person), about different items, and a run could make either miss without the other. No other MATERIAL_FAIL or MINOR_GAP exists outside their knock-ons.

rules.requires: Each report lists every trap with the share of the weighted answer it decides and gives a line 'Failure-pattern risk: YES/NO'. The line is YES when the largest trap share is 30% or more; the report then warns that runs missing that trap fail the same rows so the baseline's failure-pattern check can fail, advises 2-3 independent traps and links the failure patterns guide, section 4. Below the 30% line there is no warning.

If most runs miss it, they fail the same rows and the baseline's failure-pattern check can fail. Consider spreading the difficulty: 2–3 independent traps in other parts of the task, each with its own deciding record. See the [failure patterns guide, section 4](/?guide=patterns#4-build-at-least-three-traps-that-split-the-rollouts).
- Largest share: T1 ≈33% (30% or more). T1–T4 all change the total and shares, so runs that miss any one of them fail the same total/share/reply rows. They're told apart only by their own item rows.

rules.requires: A rubric title may not exceed 120 words. fixcheck applies the cap to every candidate row, and a patched title that goes over 120 words is restructured.

excerpts.text: Every fix is in the Fix List with its mark. - Keep the title at or under 120 words, and update the evidence's Accept text to match.

rules.requires: Every fix is checked with an opposite-pair test, attributed to rubric_flow_v2: a fix for one defect must not create the other. When two findings pull in opposite directions the fix has to satisfy both, and a fix that would create the opposite defect is not taken.

excerpts.text: rubric_flow_v2 says "A fix for one must not create the other", so the submitted wording stays. Under it, the share-then-move and other-folder-then-move paths fail, and the never-moved case is graded once, by R1.
- This carve-out settles run 1's opposite finding (an ambiguous "already done"). The opposite-pair rule in `rubric_flow_v2.md` requires the fix to satisfy both.
- R5 split lines (R5 pass): fixing it would make R5 fail together with R16/R18 on the same split error, creating a cascade (opposite-pair rule).

about: Rules the platform applies that the local Evals/ and claude/ copies do not hold, taken from stored platform reports because the platform release cannot be obtained. 'rules' is curated by hand; 'reports', 'releases', 'spec_hashes' and 'names' are rebuilt by tools/release_drift.py.
date_note: Platform /rubric reports and some /oe and /hardness reports print no review date. For those, dates in 'rules' were estimated from file dates within the release's printed window and may be off by a day or two; the tool leaves such dates empty in 'reports', 'releases', 'spec_hashes' and 'names'.
